<!-- section:action -->

1. **Look at what is blurred.** If the moving subject is soft and the background is sharp, the subject moved. If everything is soft in the same direction, the camera moved. If nothing is sharp anywhere, the focus missed.
2. **Change one setting for that cause.** Subject motion: a shorter shutter duration. Camera movement: support the camera or shorten the duration. Missed focus: refocus, because a shorter duration will not help.
3. **Account for the light you gave up.** A shorter duration admits less light; open the aperture, add light or accept a darker frame, as the [capture lesson](#/lesson/photo-m01-l01/photo-m01-l01-understand) explains.
4. **Judge the result at the intended viewing size** before calling the problem fixed.

<!-- section:example -->

### Worked example: a fictional park race

At 1/60 s a runner is soft while the finish banner behind is crisp, so the runner moved, not the camera. The runner covers about 6 metres per second, so at 1/60 s the runner travels about 100 mm during the exposure and at 1/500 s about 12 mm. The photographer changes only the shutter duration, to 1/500 s. That admits about eight times less light, three stops, so the aperture opens three stops, from f/8 to f/2.8. The new frame shows a sharp runner at phone size.

<!-- section:template -->

### Your blur diagnosis

| --------------- | ------------ | ---------- | -------------- | ---------------------- |
|                 |              |            |                |                        |

<!-- section:limits -->

This guide separates three common causes. It does not cover lens softness, the interaction with image stabilization or deliberate motion blur, where the blur is the intention.
